div.head: Introduction
div.p: A city without lights has become almost unimaginable in today's world. It is widely accepted that light provides increased security and safety, both objectively and perceptually (Boyce, 2019). It can also extend the day which is beneficial for our economic nighttime environment, and it can attract our attention towards beautiful scenes (Boyce, 2019). However, it has also been shown that artificial light at night (ALAN) can have negative consequences on human health and biodiversity (Davis et al., 2023;Kørner, 2023). Furthermore, energy consumption in the lighting sector is one of the most severe of all sectors (Linares Arroyo et al., 2024). In light of these recent findings, it is perhaps time to rethink the way we light our cities at night and to consider whether an abundance of lighting at night is absolutely necessary, or whether, and if so how, we can return to previous times with less ALAN. In this thesis, we explore these questions by performing a scoping review of research on darkness in urban environments. Through thematic analysis of the manuscripts from the scoping review, we will provide insights on the current state of darkness research and our current relationship with darkness. Finally, I will reflect on the findings and the question whether and how darkness should be incorporated as a design asset.

div.head: The impact of lighting on energy consumption
div.p: The area of lighting technology contributes to 20% of all energy consumption globally and 6% of CO2 emissions globally (Linares Arroyo et al., 2024). This is reason enough for the lighting industry to focus on improvements in the sustainability and efficiency of its products. One of these recent developments has been the rapid improvements of LED technology, which have been praised for their energy-saving potential, expanded lifetime, and the increased visibility they provide (De Almeida et al., 2014). This seemed to offer the opportunity to keep the lighting design in the urban context unchanged, while decreasing energy consumption, CO2 emissions, and costs associated with lighting. However, a rebound effect is taking place, which only increases energy consumption and costs of the lighting design (Fouquet & Pearson, 2012). Fouquet and Pearson explain that this is a trend which continuously can be seen in lighting research, where improvements in efficiency at first lead to a decrease in energy consumption, or costs, but that over time these reductions start increasing again, up until the point where they eventually exceed the energy consumption or costs associated with the previous technology. This effect is related to the relationship between per capita income and price elasticities of energy. When the factor associated with per capita income is smaller than the factor of price elasticity, a rebound effect will increase consumption up until the limit that citizens can permit themselves. This rebound effect is caused by rational human behavior, as Otto et al. (2014) explain. They explain rational behavior as a means of trying to satisfy personal ends. Consequently, it seems rational behavior for using technology, in this case lighting technology, is to satisfy personal needs for light, without consideration of the overall effects of said behavior. Otto et al. argue that to overcome this rational behavior, intrinsic motivation of the end-users has to change, in order for them to act "irrationally". Naturally, it seems impossible to intrinsically motivate our entire society, and rebound effects seem an inevitable outcome of technological developments in efficiency, hence a call for curtailment is being made. Curtailment of the current lighting design practices would imply that we are prohibited from using this amount of light and would have to find ways to reduce energy consumption, either in the form of dimming lights or partially shutting them off for a specified period of time.

div.head: The recognition of light pollution as a problem
div.p: With the increased usage of ALAN, several other problems beyond energy consumption have arisen. One of the mains concerns with ALAN is light pollution. Currently around 80% of the world lives under "light polluted skies" -a sky which has a brightness 8% higher than its natural sky brightness -with this number being close to 99% for Europe and North America (Falchi et al., 2016). Through satellite-based research, it has been estimated that observable light emissions increased by at least 49% from 1992 to 2017 (de Miguel et al., 2021). De Miguel et al. however suspect that, due to the spectra of LEDs being undetectable to satellites, the number might actually be somewhere between 270% and 400%. DarkSky (formerly known as the International Dark-Sky Association; IDA), a major authority in research on the negative effects of artificial light, defines light pollution as any adverse effect of artificial light. Although this term may appear broad, this definition is reasonable for DarkSky given the many applications and effects associated with artificial light, which they all want to encapsulate within a single definition. Rajkhowa (2014) describes that light pollution can be experienced in the form of trespass, over-illumination, glare, clutter, and sky-glow and can affect plants, animals, humans and astronomy. However, general consensus on what light classifies as pollution is not reached. While some common constraints are shared, lighting pollution experts and light design professionals differ in their definition of light pollution (Schulte-Römer, Meier, Dannemann, et al., 2019). According to Schulte-Römer, Meier, Dannemann et al., light pollution experts regard all light at night as pollution, whereas lighting designers look at the context to determine whether light can be seen as pollution. Lighting designers look at the usefulness or value of light and only deem quantifiable factors as problems, such as glare, trespass, and unnecessary energy consumption. Light pollution experts point more towards the negative effects that light can have on flora, fauna, humans and ecosystems, and human experiences being lost. These differences highlight the absence of a holistic approach towards the problem. A review of the scientific literature on light pollution by Rodrigo-Comino et al. (2023) revealed light pollution to be a multifaceted problem, difficult to tackle due to the many disciplines that can make impacts on lighting design. They state light pollution to be highly affected by decisions being made by stakeholders, policymakers, politicians, and local citizens. Lyytimäki and Rinne (2013) show, however, that the general public is fairly unaware about ecological and health effects of light pollution. Citizens define light pollution as hindering outdoor relaxation or recreation, a definition which is far off from the definitions given by experts in lighting.

Light pollution is more than a mere disturbance, and impacts flora, fauna, humans, and ecosystems, as light pollution experts have specified (Schulte-Römer, Meier, Dannemann, et al., 2019). Biologically, circadian rhythms are entrained to the light-dark cycle of earth spanning over the 24-h period. The implementation of ALAN, however, has impacted these circadian rhythms. In early days, the invention of artificial light was praised for the ability to lengthen the day. However, as Kørner (2023) describes, lengthening the day severely impacts the light-dark cycle we are entrained to. For virtually all organisms, our circadian rhythms are approximately 24 hours, but not exactly, and light acts as Zeitgebers for us to synchronize our internal biological clock (Davis et al., 2023). Davis et al. state that LEDs often emit excessive blue light, which is crucial for entrainment of the human circadian rhythm. This disrupts bodily systems, such as metabolism and the sleep-wake cycle, but also influences mood and cognition. Disruptions of these bodily systems can in turn lead to a vast range of problems, ranging from concentration-loss to cardiovascular diseases or increased risk of certain types of cancer (Davis et al., 2023). Davis et al. furthermore explain that alteration of the natural cycle also disturbs the biological rhythms of flora and fauna and thus impacts ecosystems. Not only the circadian rhythm of plants and animals is impacted, but also their photoperiodic timer: their ability to use the length of the day as a seasonal cue. By shifting circadian rhythms and the photoperiodic timer, animals can shift seasonal activities and can, for example, time their hibernation wrong and be awake in times when food supply is limited (Davis et al., 2023). These can be considered as the more indirect effects of light pollution on ecosystems, but ALAN can also have more direct effects. An example of this is the attraction of insects to bright lights, making them easy prey for predators, and thus decreasing the total amount of insects in an ecosystem (Kørner, 2023). A different example are migratory birds, that can be caught in upwards rising light beams (Kørner, 2023). The celestial light cues that these birds use to guide their way are almost invisible from within the beam, and as a result these birds are unable to escape the beam. Lyytimäki and Rinne (2013) have shown that the average citizen is unaware of all the potential impacts of light pollution, and this partially might be explained by basic assumptions that we have about light. "More light is always positive", is an assumption that is often heard, as well as "regulating outdoor lighting is a violation of citizen's rights" (Lyytimäki & Rinne, 2013). Lyytimäki and Rinne explain that light is associated with invention and revolution, while darkness is associated with backwardness. When citizens do get acquainted with the consequences of ALAN, it can invoke emotional responses (Breukel & Cieraad, 2024). Breukel and Cieraad tested this by designing an eco-art installation with the aim of raising awareness on light pollution as an environmental problem. Public engagement in a multifaceted problem such as this can create more awareness in the wide range of consequences of ALAN. Therefore, it is perhaps important to help the general public understand all sides of the issue, instead of merely re-emphasizing the positive associations towards light that are currently being held.

div.head: Limiting the negative effects of ALAN
div.p: Considering the negative effects of ALAN, it becomes obvious that there is a need to rethink our current lighting implementation. In 2014, Clanton proposed four simple rules on how to design urban lighting accordingly. They stated to use light only when necessary, use the lowest illuminance possible, minimize the amount of light emitted upwards, and dim or turn off lights during hours of curfew (Clanton, 2014). Light pollution experts agree with these recommendations, however, they can prove difficult to implement. When is light necessary, or what is the lowest illuminance possible in a specific situation? Falchi et al. (2011) also explained some practical implementations that try to limit the amount of light pollution. According to them luminaire design should use full shielding, limit the area of lighting, eliminate over-lighting, shut off lights when not in use, and limit the growth in lighting installations. Nevertheless, even if one were to follow all of these prescriptions, some residual light pollution scatters into the sky through reflections.

With technological advancements in LEDs, these types of luminaires were deemed as the most sustainable form of lighting (De Almeida et al., 2014;Schulte-Römer, Meier, Söding, et al., 2019). However, although LEDs indeed show are more energy-efficient, they paradoxically are not environmentally friendly. The spectrum of blue-rich WLEDs (white light emitting diodes), although being praised as most sustainable, increases the problems of light pollution significantly, as they have a high peak in blue wavelength light. Blue wavelength light has the biggest effect on circadian misalignment and photoperiodic timing (Schulte-Römer, Meier, Söding, et al., 2019) and skyglow (Bierman, 2012). Research is being done on blue-free WLEDs (white light emitting diodes), which show the same potential as the WLEDs currently in place, but limit the disruptions caused by it (Menéndez-Velázquez et al., 2022), as they emit light with hardly any blue components. Cutting down on blue components of light will affect circadian misalignment, photoperiodic timing, and skyglow less than with the current LEDs.

Both Clanton (2014) and Falchi et al. (2011) mention some form of shielding as a possible solution towards limiting light pollution and thus ALAN. Shielding offers the potential to reduce the amount of light that escapes towards the sky and causes skyglow. Kyba et al. (2021) found that with fully shielded streetlighting in the city of Tucson, Arizona, streetlights still contribute towards around 20% of light pollution. In the situation where Tucson dims its street lighting, this can be reduced towards around 13%. This shows that streetlighting alone is not the only polluter, as other sources such as advertising or facade lights also contribute towards the problems caused by ALAN. This shows that focusing on streetlighting alone will not necessarily overcome problems caused by ALAN.

Both Clanton (2014) and Falchi et al. (2011) mention another principle that limits light pollution; shutting off lights when not in use or unnecessary. This could for example be achieved using adaptive street lighting and smart street lighting systems. The biggest benefit of such a system is the energy and waste saving potential, as the streetlights will be completely shut off when no one is near them and will only turn back on towards normal once the sensors notice something on the street. However, this in itself can cause other forms of light pollution, such as light startle (see Haans, 2024). Light startle is caused by the sudden onset of streetlights and can cause residents to feel the need to check what caused the onset and potentially induce feelings of anxiety when they cannot determine the reason for the onset.

An even more drastic change that limits the negative effects of ALAN would be curtailment. This would mean that we have to drastically limit our light usage, and dim streetlights or completely shut them off during a specified period of time.

div.head: Public backlash
div.p: Publicly announcing curtailment measures, such as reducing the intensity of street lighting will, however, often result in backlash from citizens. As Lyytimäki and Rinne (2013) pointed out, citizens regard this as a violation of their rights. This is mostly because improved street lighting has been associated with reductions in crime. While some research has indeed found that improved lighting reduces crime (Welsh & Farrington, 2008), other research found mixed results. Other research suggests improved street lighting did not reduce crime but only reduced the fear of crime of citizens (Atkins et al., 1991). Furthermore, Welsh and Farrington (2008) reported that not only nighttime crime was reduced in areas with improved street lighting, but also daytime crime. Welsh and Farrington therefore conclude that street lighting might have more of an impact on community building, or the feeling of social control, than it has on actual prevention of crime. Nevertheless, it shows that the effect is not direct, and that there might be other nonlight related factors that influence it. However, while improving street lighting might have an effect on crime, the opposite effect of reducing street lighting is not so evident. Davies and Farrington (2020) found that switching off streetlights in English neighborhoods was related to differences in types of crime: where burglary and vehicle theft increased and violence on the streets decreased. Nevertheless, costs of crime did not show any significant changes, nor did criminal damage. The authors provide an explanation for this in stating that switching off street lighting might have deterred citizens from going out in the dark. Research done on power outages also suggests that total blackouts do not impact crime rates (Lal et al., 2023). The results that do show a statistically significant effect between increased lighting and reduced crime, also receive criticism that their method of testing cannot justify the claim. Marchant (2004) claims that these findings underestimate the true variability in the data, as crime events are not statistically independent, but are correlated. In this sense, Marchant suggests that crimes tend to cluster in time and space and can be committed by the same individuals. This showcases the difficulty of defining any relationship between lighting and crime, as there might be several factors influencing it.

Reductions in dimming of streetlights, however, often go largely unnoticed by the general public (Green et al., 2015;Kyba et al., 2021). Kyba et al. tested this by setting the lighting to 30%, 60%, 90% and 100% brightness on random days, receiving no comments or complaints at all from residents. Furthermore, no evidence was found that the dimming had any effect on public safety. A possible explanation for the lack of awareness for the dimming could be that the human eye is able to adapt quickly to all these situations.

These results prove the complexity of the situation, as dimming goes largely unnoticed, but does receive backlash once it is known by the public. Although the effect of light on traffic safety cannot be denied, the association that dimming streetlights decreases safety, in the form of crime or perceived safety, is strong enough to be sustained, even though citizens might not have noticed the dimming. This is no surprise, as these beliefs are sustained by professionals in the field, such as Lawrence Fennelly who states that shutting off streetlights would have an immediate effect on burglary, theft and vandalism (Fennelly, 1982). Pease (1999) reflects on this statement as pure dogmatism towards darkness. They also argue that, with such a polarized opinion and beliefs, lighting actually does prevent crime, as long as you believe it. Fennelly's opinion on the effects of shutting off streetlights is unchanged in the sixth edition of The Handbook of Loss Prevention and Crime Prevention (Fennelly, 2020). Regardless of whether one agrees with the accuracy of any of these claims, it does show that these opinions are sustained in some way.

Research has shown that providing information on the environmental opportunities could increase the acceptance of residents for reduced street lighting, however, this effect could only be found in those who already regarded environmental values as important (Boomsma & Steg, 2014). Boomsma and Steg also highlight the importance of aligning dimming strategies with citizens' values. This shows that reducing the impacts of ALAN is a sensitive matter, and compliance is needed from residents through value sensitive approaches for designing darkness into the city.

div.head: The lack of a human perspective in streetlighting design
div.p: Current street lighting design is often not focused on people's values, but on technological performance indicators (Thiel et al., 2017). Thiel et al. explain the most important performance indicators of street lighting to be choice of technology, energy efficiency, planning of allocation of resources, technical efficiency, and evaluation of the performance level (e.g., uniformity). Even though the authors conclude that management of street lighting is an important factor in human lives, a human component in evaluating the performance of street lighting is missing. An example of this can be found in the management of outdoor lighting solutions in the Swedish Planning and Building Act (PBL; Fraenkel et al., 2024). The lighting masterplans consider both daytime and nighttime lighting as one, not taking into account the differences in uses between the daytime and nighttime context. As proposed by the authors, some values that are more apparent in nocturnal context include nighttime economy, a socially viable living environment, environmental conditions, and cultural and natural values. Between daytime and nighttime conditions, these values are weighed differently and should thus be implemented differently in the lighting design (Fraenkel et al., 2024). The lack of human perspective in lighting design has furthermore been acknowledged by Amoruso et al. (2022) who did a scientific review on the human visual system and lighting theories. They found a lack of human perspective and saw that lighting design is often approached as an engineering subject. Instead, they make a proposition of how to design according to the capabilities of the human eye.

div.head: The difficulty of defining darkness
div.p: Darkness is not an easily quantifiable term. While literal darkness can be seen as the absence of light, metaphorical darkness can have many implications, such as evil, but also mystery (Barkman, 2010). Barkman (2010) speaks about aesthetical and ethical injustice against darkness. According to him, darkness is often grasped as a single term, not differentiating between literal and metaphorical darkness. This causes the associations towards metaphorical darkness to flow over in those for literal darkness. While Barkman introduces two aspects of darkness, Dunn & Edensor (2023) explain darkness as multiple and situational. Darkness is shaped by much more than its literal or metaphorical definition but is also shaped by weather conditions and affordances in landscape. A clear sky with moonlight translates towards different darkness than darkness during a cloudy night. The same is true for landscape affordances; trees in a forest that block the light generate different darkness than the darkness on an open field. Next to that, darkness is also shaped by seasonal variations and geographical location (Tainio, 2024). Based on the season and latitude, darkness occurs more frequently, showcasing that it has a temporal dynamic. In its essence, darkness can also be seen as paradoxical (Dunn & Edensor, 2023). The term dark skies include both the darkness surrounding the earth, granting us the ability to see stars, but also the darkness concealing these views. In other words, both a sky filled with stars, as well as a vast emptiness of nothingness are spoken of as dark skies.

All these concepts make darkness difficult to quantify, and thus difficult to put as an asset. There is also a substantial difference between rural darkness and urban darkness. While conclusions drawn from research on rural darkness are often based on therapeutic wilderness sessions and talk about darkness as something to be experienced "out there" (Erichsen, 2024;Frey, 2007;Tonetti, 2024), urban darkness does not possess these qualities. In rural context, darkness is something that people seek to experience, while in urban context, darkness is a state of the environment that people are forced to deal with when going out. This alone makes it that rural darkness is a choice, while urban darkness is typically a condition. If urban darkness is simply defined as absence of light, it is unmeasurable, as absence is non-quantifiable. With the over-illumination of cities, Edensor (2015) fears that we are losing our relationship with darkness. As we are growing more habituated towards ubiquitous illumination in the city, it grows harder and harder to imagine the nights as they once were, diminishing our relationship with darkness. In order for us to make substantial changes towards lighting design and its adverse effects, we should be aware of the relationship that we have with darkness, showing the importance of finding a contextually right definition for urban darkness. For the sake of this research, it is important to consider the boundaries of what aspects of darkness we take into account. As the definitions between literal and metaphorical darkness flow over in each other, both will be considered to a certain extent. While we are not interested in illuminance levels, we are interested in the feelings that darkness evokes after the sun has set. In this sense, we consider literal darkness as the setting of the sun, while metaphorical darkness is the aspect of feelings. This takes into account the psychological factors, contextuality, and temporality of darkness. As a working definition for urban darkness, it is therefore classified as the contextual state of the environment, and the feelings it evokes, after the sun has begun to settle.

div.head: Purpose of this study
div.p: The aim of this research is to map out what research has been done on darkness in the urban environment and to determine our current relationship with it. As seen, both light pollution and darkness can be seen as a multifaceted problem which have many aspects involved. To determine all the aspects that should be taken into account, the first part of this research will be a scoping review, aimed at retrieving valuable research into attitudes, values, perceptions, or experiences of darkness. The scoping review follows the following two research questions: (1) What research is done on pedestrian's definitions, values, and perceptions of darkness or the absence of street lighting in the urban environment, and (2) Which measurement methods have been used to measure the abovementioned concepts. The second part of this research will be thematic analysis on the definition of darkness and our relationship to it, according to the articles found in the scoping review. The first research question aims to develop an understanding of what current research has already found on our relationship towards darkness, while the second research question aims to explore in what way we currently measure our appraisal of darkness. This master thesis serves as a base for understanding concepts explored in the Art of Darkness (European Commission, 2024) project, which is aiming at developing a quantitative measurement tool for darkness appraisal.

Since darkness is a multifaceted term, this means there should be boundaries present to limit the number of articles that qualify for the scoping review. For this, we used the PCC (population -concept -context) framework, which helps in defining research questions for scoping reviews (JBI, 2024). It can be argued that the experience of natural darkness is too dissimilar from the experience of urban darkness for research on the former to inform about the latter, hence the context of this project is on the urban environment. The main concept used in the scoping review is darkness. It was chosen to keep the concept rather broad, given the various implementations of darkness. For the population, we chose to focus on pedestrians only. While darkness is also an important topic in traffic safety (e.g., in autonomous vehicle detection), we wanted to focus solely on the human perspective of designing with darkness as the moral and aesthetic roles of how citizens interpret darkness in their environment is crucial for adaptation of the lighting design to limit light pollution. We choose to only focus on pedestrians since they are the slowest form of traffic. Cars and bikes have a higher speed and carry lights of their own, making them less affected by the darkness. Pedestrians do not carry lights and are more surrounded by the darkness. For cars and bikes, darkness in this sense has to do with traffic safety, e.g., not seeing obstacles, while for pedestrians, we hypothesize that darkness has more of an effect on internal attitudes or feelings.

div.head: Scoping review
div.p: The scoping review was conducted according to the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews; Tricco et al., 2018) and the JBI manual on how to conduct scoping reviews (JBI, 2024). The scoping review aimed to adhere to the checklist developed in the PRISMA-ScR, as far as the items were relevant inclusions for this master thesis. Because of time constraints and since we were interested in the breadth of articles that covers this topic, no critical appraisal of the included sources was done.

div.head: Eligibility criteria
div.p: In order to filter out which articles were relevant for the research question, eligibility criteria were set up. Only articles that focused on opinions, values, attitudes, or feelings towards darkness by pedestrians were considered, given that they included a scope towards the urban context. Research papers were not excluded based on the type of research that was done, and no empirical research method had to be present. As darkness is a broad topic, exclusion reasons were also determined, to make sure that articles could be assessed correctly. Articles were excluded if they focused solely on ecology, traffic accidents or (fast) mobility, actual safety or crime rates, were not focused on the urban context or streetlights, reviewed policies currently in place, or focused predominantly on the technological aspects of lighting design, such as illuminance level for facial recognition over a specified distance.

div.head: Information sources
div.p: The databases included were Scopus and Web of Science. We have chosen these databases for their amount of peer reviewed, high-quality articles and scientific relevance, as opposed to other databases. Furthermore, both Scopus and Web of Science offer the possibility to use advanced search queries, which are crucial in filtering out irrelevant literature. Unpublished literature was not considered, and reference lists of included literature were not screened, for sake of time. The final search of literature was conducted on the 4th of March 2025.

div.head: Search strategy
div.p: Developing the search query was an iterative process to determine which terms worked, and which terms yielded many insignificant results. For both Scopus and Web of Science, the final search query can be found in Appendix A. Instead of the chosen variables for the first part of the query, several synonyms were considered. Two variables that yielded more search results but were eventually excluded were 'values' and 'views'. We have chosen to exclude these variables due to their polysemous meanings. Furthermore, this was also done for the variable 'dim*', which resulted in way too many insignificant results.

div.head: Data collection
div.p: Screening of the literature was done using the Rayyan software, which enables for structured literature reviews. As per the PRISMA-ScR, screening consisted of two rounds: first Title-Abstract screening, followed by Full-text screening. Screening was done by two researchers independently. One researcher first removed all articles that were clearly off topic. The remaining entries were examined by both researchers. Articles that resulted in conflict between both researchers were discussed in a specified meeting along with a third researcher. For both the first and second round of screening, the same inclusion and exclusion criteria were used. Articles that could not be found due to accessibility reasons were excluded from the final list.

div.head: Data charting
div.p: For data charting, MS Excel was used. For each article, the following items were extracted: Title, Author, Publication year, Publication country, Type of paper, Empirical method (if applicable), Data collection method (if applicable), Demographic participants (if applicable), Measurement instrument for darkness evaluation. When one of these items was not present in the source (e.g., non-empirical papers not having participants), it was noted down as NA. Data charting was only done by the main researcher.

div.head: Thematic Analysis
div.p: The result of the scoping review provided a list of manuscripts that focused on darkness research. In order to synthesize the data in there, thematic analysis was used to group similar concepts within and between papers. Using thematic analysis, key-phrases were established, after which codes were constructed, which translated to themes. This development from key-phrase to code to themes ensured that themes provided interpretive insights which were true to the data of the manuscripts. Using these themes, insights were developed towards an understanding of our current relationship with darkness. Thematic analysis was conducted using the MAXQDA software, which is useful for qualitative analysis because of its well-designed coding structures and the possibilities of the program. The thematic analysis was conducted according to the guidelines set by Naeem et al. (2023), to ensure credibility and consistency. The step-by-step process can be seen in Figure 1. (Naeem et al., 2023) 2.2.1 Familiarizing with the data All articles have been re-read, and non-relevant sections were marked in red, creating snippets of data that were important. In the remainder of the text, relevant pieces of text were highlighted using different colors. After reading each article, a list of potential codes for the article was proposed, and a memo was added in MAXQDA showcasing important notes and my own reflection on the article after reading it. The list of potential codes serves as an initial coding system.

div.head: Selection of keywords
div.p: Although Naeem et al. (2023) specify that the next step in the thematic analysis process would be to select keywords, this step is not performed as strict as to their guidelines. They define keyword selection as the crucial parts of information that summarize the data. Upon initial selection of keywords, we noticed that a lot of context in these keywords was lost. For thematic analysis of larger pieces of text, it might therefore be better to not make a selection of keywords, but rather use key paragraphs or sentences, so the context is kept within the data. In this case, key-phrase selection serves as a method of summarizing larger pieces of text, keeping the context within the smaller pieces of data that are key-phrases.

div.head: Coding
div.p: In order to develop codes, the key-phrases of articles were re-read and developed into descriptive codes. These codes can be seen as short summaries that encapsulate the meaning of key-phrases. Similarity between the initial coding system developed in the familiarization phase, and this coding system was assessed, and codes were merged into one system. Codes were then assessed to determine whether they encapsulated all key-phrases within them, leading to the second iteration of codes (for example: constraints, paradoxes and comfort all merged into challenges). In this iteration process, several codes were also transitioned towards subcodes of a larger code group (e.g., 'Connectedness to place' and 'Connectedness to people' becoming subcodes of a larger code; 'Connectedness'). These codes were critically assessed on clarity for the third iteration stage, which led to the eventual coding system (for example: challenges transitioning towards darkness as an asset and limited space). How this process visually was done is partially shown in Appendix B.

div.head: Theme development
div.p: The codes were transferred to the MIRO software, where they were placed as sticky notes with a density corresponding the number of times the code was used (see Figure 2). MIRO enables for a visual inspection of relationship between codes and made it accessible to test how codes could relate to each other in becoming themes. Themes were developed first as descriptive themes, where they reflected the codes and data well. For the second iteration of the themes, these were written out including some examples from the data, to assess whether the theme truly reflected the data. Themes were then adjusted to match the data by either changing the themes or adding/removing codes associated with the theme. Several themes that were too similar were combined into one theme, changing them from being descriptive towards interpretive. For the third iteration of themes, these steps were repeated.

Figure 2: Theme development according to density of codes 2.2.5 Conceptualization In the conceptualization phase, themes are further refined according to existing theory and defined within theoretical terms. According to Naeem et al. (2023), concepts refer to any mental representation of underlying social structure. For this research, the relationship between themes and existing research was explored as part of the discussion. The relationships between themes were assessed using the questions charted by Naeem et al. (2023) to see whether they encapsulated the data and provided meaningful insights that explained the underlying message of themes.

div.head: Development of conceptual model
div.p: Although Naeem et al. (2023) describe the sixth step to be the development of a conceptual model, this development or justification of a conceptual model was outside the scope of this paper.

div.head: Results
div.p: Figure 3 presents the PRISMA-flowchart for the scoping review. From the two databases included, 2468 unique sources of evidence were found. Through title-abstract screening 2429 articles were removed. The PRISMAflowchart provides a list of examples for exclusion reasons. As both researchers used the labels slightly different, no count for the exact usage of a label is provided. Eventually, 39 articles were full-text screened, which resulted in 15 more exclusions. In this phase, exclusions were mostly for accessibility reasons, where the article was unable to be accessed from within the TU/e library database. Other examples of exclusions were one article being written in French instead of English, one record being only an abstract (of a poster presentation), and several articles having the wrong scope, by focusing too much on the effects of light or on rural darkness. This eventually yielded a total amount of 24 studies being included in the thematic analysis part of this research.

div.head: Descriptive statistics
div.p: Appendix C shows the table of all included articles. There were 44 different authors contributing to these 24 different manuscripts. Most authors were only present in one entry, but there were a few that were present in more, those being Taylor Stone and Mette Hvass each with five entries, and Nick Dunn and Ellen Kathrine Hansen with three entries each. The articles included were mostly theoretical papers, however, we also found several case studies and studies based on empirical evidence, showing the range of research conducted in this field. Most research was Western-Europe-based, however, there were also four entries from the United States and one from China. Figure 4 shows the distribution of research throughout Europe. Most research can be classified in the domain of environmental sciences, with six manuscripts being from the conference series "Earth & Environmental Scienes". Other often included domains are ethics, geography, and urban planning. Interestingly, only one article specifically mentions the domain of lighting design. Figure 5 shows the distribution of publication years. As can be seen from Figure 5, urban darkness is a very recent research topic, as no entries before 2013 were found, and the majority of articles ranged from 2022 and later. The last column in the table from Appendix C includes the measurement instruments used for darkness evaluation. Most articles did not mention an instrument of any kind. There were a few that mentioned (walk-along) interviews as the best measurement instrument for darkness appraisal, but wat becomes most evident is that there is no unified way for how to measure evaluation of darkness. Most authors include some form that they see most fit for the situation, or that they have experience with, rather than that there is a standardized way for how to assess this.

div.head: Themes
div.p: Figure 6 shows the table of themes. It distinguishes between main themes and sub-themes. Subthemes are attached to the main theme they are corresponding with. In the following section, the themes and sub-themes will be explained in the order in which they are presented on the table. In text, main themes are written in bold, while subthemes are written both in bold and italic. Themes are numbered according to the order of the table in Figure 6, where sub-themes are numbered according to the main theme they belong to.
0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 2013 2015 2018 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025Publication years Theme 1: Perceptions of darkness shift across cultures, people, situations, and time.

How darkness is perceived really depends on the situation where it is presented. Hvass (2024) highlights this by specifying the need for context-specific lighting; as being able to enhance the existing spatial and social qualities of a space. The contextual meaning of darkness is furthermore highlighted by Stone (2018) who specifies that: "darkness is not a concrete thing but rather an evaluative consideration that directs understandings of, and relationship with, the world at night. Yet at the same time it is a real, tangible thing accessible to direct experience" (p. 7). Additionally, perception of darkness is highly dependent upon individual differences, as associations towards darkness are neither culturally nor historically universal (Edensor, 2013). This shows perception of darkness changes between, but also within subjects, from situation to situation. Next to that, darkness has temporal characteristics, both in the forms of seasonal variations and timing of darkness. As an example, Rathsach and Hvass (2022) highlight the city of Anholt, Denmark. Anholt uses the light reflected from the moon to provide visibility at night, instead of implementing streetlights. Due to the phasing of the moon, people experience bright, semi-bright, and dark nights, altering their perception of how dark the city is. Lastly, landscape can have an effect on darkness, as some regions are simply ill-suited for DarkSky site placements, just because of their sky quality (Pan et al., 2025).
Theme 2: Visual perception of darkness is not absolute but shaped by adaptation.

Our perceptions of darkness are not absolute, which makes it difficult to compare situations. We are able to adapt to darkness, both perceptually and psychologically. This adaptation process shapes our perception of how dark an environment appears. This theme consists of two sub-themes, which explain these adaptations:

div.head: Sub-theme 2.1: Perceptual adaptation allows our eyes to adjust over time and in relation to contrast.
div.p: Our eyes have the ability to adapt to darkness. In other words, our visual system slowly adjusts to increase visibility. This process demands time, however. Whereas adaptation to light happens within seconds, adaptation towards darkness takes several minutes to return to normal visual sensitivity (Amoruso et al., 2022). When illuminance levels are static, we are able to perceive the environment as less dark over time due to this adaptation. When illuminance levels change, we also adapt to these levels to maintain functional vision, although the quality and detail of what we perceive may shift. These sensitivity changes of the eye have to be accounted for when designing with darkness (Amoruso et al., 2022). However, the adaptation process also makes it difficult to compare perceptions of darkness between situations and people, as it is difficult to take individuals' level of adaptation into account. Furthermore, our perception of darkness is dependent upon the contrasts introduced. High contrast areas can create the experience of very dark areas. Reducing this contrast will also shift the perception of how dark the darkest area appears (Hvass, 2024).

div.head: Sub-theme 2.2: Psychological adaptation alters our sense of how dark an environment appears over time.
div.p: We have difficulties comparing darkness between days. This is because it is difficult to judge whether an environment looks equally dark as it normally does, or in other words, as the baseline scenario. This is called shifting baseline syndrome (Lyytimäki, 2015). Lyytimäki (2015) explains this as follows: "The concept of shifting baseline syndrome refers to the changing human perceptions of the state of certain system due to loss of experience of past conditions. Based on their personal experiences, people may consider the current situation to be the typical or normal state, even when the system has changed considerably compared to earlier states" (p. 8). According to Stone (2021b), this can happen both within people and over generations. Within people, it means that we have forgotten about past experiences and judge the current situation to be the same as past ones. Over generations, this happens when past experiences are not passed on to new generations. Both these processes show how we are able to psychologically adjust our baseline to what we deem as "normal".
Theme 3: Our cities are designed solely for humans and cause us to become disconnected from the more-than-human world, which urban darkness could help restore.

It can be argued that the problems of light pollution are symptoms of an underlying problem: disconnection (Lam, 2020). As we are implementing more light in the designs of our cities, this results in consequences for non-human lifeforms (see the examples in Section 1.2). Although these consequences are recognized, they are often placed second to human interest (Tainio, 2023). Cities are anthropogenic in nature, they are designed by humans, for humans. Next to that, cities have become synonymous with light, and we cannot imagine the city without it (Dunn, 2020b). Stone (2021a) explains this dependency as that "It implies that to have a truly dark sky-to be devoid of light pollution, and artificial light in general-cities also need to be devoid of human activity" (p. 10). This statement implies that we simply cannot exist anymore without lighting in our cities and that city lights and night sky have come into conflict. With this, cities have also come into conflict with other lifeforms inhabiting them. Shaw (2015) explains these clashes as being part of a 'contact zone', where the behavior and roles of nocturnal species emerge from their interactions, rather than existing independently. If humans enter this nocturnal world, they get entangled in the web of interactions, which currently causes clashes. Shaw explains that therefore synergistic rewilding of the night can lead to urban restoration. Synergistic rewilding in this sense would mean rewilding our nights -to let go of human influence in dark areas -in a way that suits all users. Dill (2022) proposes to do this through designated ecosystem strips within the city, leading to more natural flow between cities and nature, and leading to less conflict between species. Challéat et al. (2021) agrees with this, but stresses that these should be dynamic to account for the temporal nature of darkness. This could for example mean turning lights off during hunting times for nocturnal predators and switching the lights back on when these animals are no longer active in that fraction of the night.
Theme 4: Our current appreciation and design approaches to darkness rely on large, uninterrupted areas, which pushes it outside the city and reduces our access to it.

As mentioned by Amoruso et al. (2022), to provide for non-noticeable shifts in darkness through the adaptive abilities of the eye, this would require large areas of space, since our eyes take time to adapt to darkness, and smaller areas would lead to a less gradual decrease in illumination levels, which we would notice. Even though denoted as an inalienable right to everyone, for a majority of the world this leads to darkness no longer being accessible within the city, as these areas do not fit in the city. To increase this accessibility, DarkSky aims at preservation through parks or reserves. DarkSky parks have a threshold for DarkSky quality, which requires them to, among other things, have a maximum level of skyglow. This requirement causes many parks to be substantially large that they need to be placed outside of the city too, however. This decreases their connectivity, which eventually results in impaired efficiency of the parks (Pan et al., 2025). According to Pan et al. regions with high urban development and population density are ill-suited for DarkSky parks. Nevertheless, it is possible to bring darkness into the city, just not with the DarkSky quality necessary for parks. This would result in unscenic darkness in the city, which is more difficult to enjoy as it demands an understanding of what happens in the shadows (Tainio, 2023). Additionally, the corridors between darkness and the city need to be well-maintained, as not to cause too large contrasts. Darkness should gradually be introduced, however, this again leads to large areas needing to be covered. Amoruso et al. (2022) explain that "it is logical to question whether it is possible to identify a clear taxonomy of areas where darkness is preserved by zooming in the urban environment" (p. 11). This shows that our current understanding of darkness limits us in design opportunities.

div.head: Sub-theme 4.1: We only appreciate exceptional darkness, and not average darkness.
div.p: In our current understanding of darkness, we often associate it with starry night skies. A loss of the night often implies our disability to see the stars in the skies. Starry night skies contribute towards sublime experiences. Stone (2021b) captures the range of emotions as feelings of awe and wonder, but also of humility, immensity and vastness. As Lam (2020) states: "We do not need to be trained stargazers and astronomers to be impressed by the star-filled skies; when anyone looks up, opens themselves to the star-filled skies, they will be moved by it" (p. 16). This pictures how stars are, according to Latour's Actor-Network theory, actors, as they can influence our emotions and behavior (Latour, 2005). This, however, also explains why we are only able to appreciate exceptional darkness, instead of average darkness around us. Average darkness -the regular darkness on a street -is not moving for the general public (Tainio, 2023). As Tainio (2023) denotes "unscenic nature may demand some effort to understand its structure and function. This cognitive undertaking allows the widening and deepening of one's perspective, which may bring forth the subtle aesthetic values of the unscenic environment. Knowing the ecological dependencies between the seemingly uninteresting vegetation, various animal species, and a specific place can turn dull streetside shrubs into an aesthetically significant environment." (p. 9). Tainio addresses average darkness as that which we are accustomed to in cities; where we can not see the stars on the sky. They explain that, to resolve light pollution problems, we should get familiar with mundane darkness and learn to appreciate life in the shadows, understanding how different conditions can shape the particularity of the nighttime environment. Even when reducing the amount of light in the city, starry night skies -and thus sublime darkness -may not exist within the city. This leads to Tainio noting that appreciating mundane darkness is a necessity. Without the appreciation of average darkness, large areas are indeed required for darkness preservation.
Theme 5: Through our lighting we try to treat places the same at night as during the day, although the identity of the environment shifts with the time of day.

As mentioned by Fraenkel et al. (2024; see section 1.5), lighting masterplans often treat day-and nighttime environments as one. However, it can be argued that places during the day and night support a different social environment, so treating them the same will not result in an identical perceived social environment. Dunn (2020a) explains it as; "places are partly defined by the social relations that occur both in and across them, which at night are far less frequent as many spaces are devoid of people" (p. 7). So, as places are devoid of people, social structure changes, but our lighting aims at extending the day into the night. Places are not static environments; there are ecological processes within a place itself that ever evolve its identity, but the definition of a place will also change when one engages with it, proving the dynamic nature of a place (Dunn, 2020a). This dynamic nature gives the place an identity; there are different inhabitants or occupants of the space and the ecological and social structure adapts accordingly. High luminous contrast differences will make the perception of all social qualities of a space impossible however and homogenous uniform light will wipe away the nighttime identity of a place by cloaking it under a bed of light (Hvass & Hansen 2022;Hvass et al., 2022). By balancing the hierarchy of lighting layers and introducing darkness as a counterpart to light, different coexistences of light and dark are able to constitute towards the nighttime identity of a place (Griffiths et al., 2023).
Theme 6: Psychological barriers shape our engagement with darkness.

Our engagement with darkness is partially limited by our psychological representation of darkness. As established, our current appreciation for darkness is in the range of starry night skies and average darkness, which is often the case in dense urban places, is difficult to understand. The following three subthemes explain how our current understanding of darkness shapes our behavior towards it.

div.head: Sub-theme 6.1: People don't enter dark places because this is not rational behavior.
div.p: Cities and light have become interdependent on one another. Dunn (2020b) explains that "urban environments have become synonymous with the functional lighting layouts that were installed" (p. 4). This makes it that we are not accustomed to the darkness at night. Stone (2021b) adds to this that the darkness caused by temporary blackouts in a city seems unreal; it is something that we cannot imagine anymore and do not know how to deal with. Because of this, it is not within our rational behavior to enter dark places. However, once people do enter these dark places, they state that it is not as scary as they expected (Vuorenmaa et al., 2024). In an experiment by Vuorenmaa et al., participants were interviewed in a walk-along interview through the neighborhood, where they also visited a dark forest at night. From afar, participants mentioned that they would have never thought about entering it, but from within, they were surprised by the visibility, and it felt less weird to enter such places from now on. Entering dark places being irrational behavior also comes from our associations with darkness, which are deeply embedded within modern society.
Sub-theme 6.2: Our negative associations with darkness are deeply embedded within modern society.

Historically seen, we have aimed at banishing darkness from the city through our lighting design. While in the beginning there was some resistance to this banishing, for centuries now we have accepted that darkness is not part of our city design. In the same way, lighting is linked to progress and urban development. Stone (2021b) explains that the "lighting-as-safe and darkness-as-dangerous associations are deeply embedded perceptions" (p. 8). As they have been reinforced for centuries, it will not be easy to seize these associations from our thoughts. Additionally, these negative associations may even lead to nyctophobia -fear of the night -for some. This adds to the difficulty of breaking these associations, as for some it has developed into more than just associations. Nyctophobia is not universally shared and similar for people, adding to the complexity darkness perception (Edensor, 2013). Our negative associations towards darkness influence our behavior, which can lead to resistance towards darkness.

div.head: Sub-theme 6.3: Resistance to darkness comes not from the dimmed environment itself, but from the absence of choice to engage with it and the mental image we have of it.
div.p: Announced dimming strategies often lead to public resistance. Edensor (2013) explains this with an example: "Responses to these disruptions to the customary ubiquity of pervasive illumination have been angry, exemplified by one local newspaper alleging that such policies heralded a 'return to the dark ages'" (p. 1). This shows that resistance towards dimming is primarily based on expectations of these policies, rather than on the actual situation itself. As Edensor states, these policies are alleged to contribute towards a return to the dark ages, showcasing the negative associations and mental image we have attached to darkness in the city. The fact that resistance comes mostly from the mental image is supported by Hvass' (2024) claim that citizens had not noticed the unannounced dimming in their neighborhood. Shaw (2015) adds in another dimension to this concept, by explaining that choice to enter the environment also influences acceptance. In their research, they conclude that "darkness can create a positive affective atmosphere where individuals have had choice over their ability to enter in[to it], but there seems to be a reverse process occurring where individuals do not have this power" (p. 6). This shows that the presence of choice to engage with darkness influences our acceptance of it. In dimming policies, we are often left with absence of choice to engage with increased darkness, leading to resistance. However, these findings also show that we can get more accustomed to darkness. Stone (2021b) claims that radical or abrupt changes will likely result in concern and will not be socially accepted, but slow steady changes might make us more familiar with darkness on a subconscious level.
Theme 7: Focusing solely on light pollution will limit the adverse effects of ALAN but does not reflect the benefits that increasing darkness has.

Focusing solely on limiting the adverse effects of light such as glare, light trespass, and skyglow will reduce the load on the environment, but is a one-sided solution. Limiting these effects will likely result in defining a threshold. However, these thresholds do not say anything about the positive values that darkness might have in certain situations. Stone (2024) explains this well by stating that "Darkness is typically defined as the partial or total absence of light, which says very little about the qualities of darkness itself" (p. 8). This shows the one-sided view we have towards lighting. Additionally, solutions that incorporate these benefits of darkness will likely be more effective in urban restoration and enjoyment of stars in the skies (Stone, 2018). Furthermore, by these adverse effects reflect us humans, but do not say anything about negative effects of light on ecosystems. Pan et al. (2025) explain that DarkSky places can contribute to gaining an understanding of the other adverse effects of light pollution by showing the benefits of darkness on ecosystems. These benefits of darkness can be classified as three subthemes attached to this theme:
Sub-theme 7.1: In darkness we are able to express ourselves and be authentic, allowing us to be connected to ourselves and others.

Darkness provides a cloak of privacy, in which we can be our authentic selves. Historically seen, darkness symbolized the place where those with diverse thoughts gathered, those who had to be overcome in order to provide a city of rationalized, liberal and responsible citizens (Edensor, 2013). Darkness provided a cloak for those citizens who did not fit this standard and allowed them to be themselves. This also allows for a deeper connection between those in the darkness (Dill, 2022). These opportunities for deeper connection are highlighted by Challéat et al. (2021) as well, who phrase it that "cultural geography studies emphasize the extent to which darkness makes possible original forms of conviviality and intimacy, the occupation of public spaces, and the perception of the world through senses other than sight" (p. 3). This showcases the unique benefits of darkness in terms of connectedness and intimacy.
Sub-theme 7.2: Darkness is good for our health.

As stated earlier in section 1.2, light at night disrupts the synchronization of our biological clock. For a strong, healthy entrainment, we need to be exposed to a strong contrast between light and dark over the 24-hour cycle (Schmal et al., 2020). In this sense, it can be argued that darkness thus has health benefits, as it does not disrupt our synchronization and melatonin secretion, whereas light does (Challéat et al., 2021). Next to direct health benefits, Dill (2022) also argues that darkness is good for psychological wellbeing, as they explain that "perceptions of natural beauty produce declinations in cortisol levels, increase subjective wellbeing, and elicit feelings of connectedness between subjects and the broader, more-than-human and cosmic world" (p. 6). This connection to the more-than-human cosmic world leads to the third benefit:

Sub-theme 7.3: Darkness allows us to have a spiritual connection and stay connected to our heritage. Griffiths et al. (2023) explain how darkness helps in putting humans in the more-than-human world, allowing us to be moved by myths and mythologies. Ancient cultures were often moved by these dark skies, which inspired them to create these myths (Alva et al., 2025). As Stone (2018) states, "The loss of the night also implies the loss of this heritage, and darkness at night is the precondition through which continued access is possible" (p. 11). This shows the spiritual connection with our ancestors through stories that darkness can enable. Darkness provides other benefits as well, such as ecological restoration, however, these three subthemes show benefits that are only true for us humans.
Theme 8: Because we are rarely required to engage with darkness, we overlook its complexities and fail to give it moral value.

We are not accustomed to being in the dark, and because of this, we are not aware of all its complexities and values, which results in us not being able to give it a moral value which accounts for these complexities and values. The average citizen does not recognize all adverse effects caused by light pollution. While disturbances such as glare or skyglow are noticeable, it is far more difficult to recognize ecological effects or ecosystems disruptions. With public engagement, and learning about darkness, we are more able to understand all facets of darkness. Tainio (2023) explains this as a necessity to create an intimate relationship with the environment, in order to assimilate all its features. In order for us to better understand darkness, Stone (2021b) argues that darkness should be encapsulated as an umbrella term, encompassing its various environmental concerns and placing it as a moral obligation to take into account. They argue that "this creates an important shift in the burden of proof-to show why not to incorporate the obligation, and give justifiable cause for that choice" (p. 10). In other words, Stone proposes that we have to shift our thinking around, not as to why light should be included, but why it is justifiable to get rid of darkness. Such moral obligations force us to understand all facets and effects of darkness and increase potential for resolving issues such as accessibility to nature (Stone, 2021a). Yet, understanding all facets and effects of darkness is a complex process. The complexity of darkness is further explained by the two subthemes:

div.head: Sub-theme 8.1: Any exploration of darkness's value necessarily involves its relationship with artificial light.
div.p: Stone (2024) explained darkness to be often characterized as an absence of light, which shows the dependency of the two. Darkness and light are both complementary and contradictory; one cannot exist without the other, but the existence of the one diminishes the other. This also means that only through our lighting design can we influence urban darkness. Any approach for designing with darkness must therefore take into account this mediating effect of light on darkness (Stone, 2021b). Edensor (2013) explains for example, that light is the most alluring when situated against darkness, thus showing the dependency of darkness on light perception.

div.head: Sub-theme 8.2: Enhancing darkness to support one value inevitably affects the extent to which other values are realized.
div.p: The values of darkness are reciprocal in nature, they all affect each other (Stone, 2018). Stone explains this in the sense that, setting darkness as a goal for one value (e.g., darkness as a goal to increase sustainability), it will also create conditions which affect other values of darkness. Another example of this relationship can be given in setting darkness as a goal for economic efficiency. While darkness has both energy-and cost savings potential, it has also been linked with negatively impacting nighttime economy (Dunn, 2020). This shows how the values of darkness cannot be enhanced independently.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: The aim of this research was to map out the breadth of research done on urban darkness using a scoping review. Based on the manuscripts included, our aim was to establish the current state of our understanding of darkness, both in terms of research and how we engage with it in our everyday lives. Section 3 provides the descriptive statistics for the manuscripts included and the themes that were developed from the data. The following section aims at establishing relationships between themes and interpreting how they shape our current relationship with darkness.

div.head: Relation between themes
div.p: As Lam (2020) has argued, the problems caused by light pollution are symptoms of the underlying problem of disconnection. In the relationship between themes, disconnection can also be seen as the root which connects other themes. Disconnection to darkness influences our psychological barriers that shape our engagement. As we are disconnected from darkness, we are unsure of how to engage with it. This results in us behaving according to our learned associations. Behaving according to these learned associations can be seen as rational behavior, which in turn makes engaging with darkness irrational behavior. Our disconnectedness to darkness also causes us to be rarely required to engage with it. Several authors have established that in recent times we have banished darkness from the city (Dunn, 2020;Lam, 2020;Stone, 2021b;Edensor, 2013). This has caused not only disconnection but also increased the rarity of us being required to engage with darkness. Since we are so rarely required to engage with darkness, it can be seen as logical that it does not fit within our rational behavior. Furthermore, when curtailment measures are announced, it also explains why we want to resist it. As the sub-theme itself already described, resistance comes not from the darkness itself, but from our mental image and the lack of choice we have to engage with it. This suggests how in a sense, the subthemes from the theme Psychological barriers shape our engagement with darkness seem to be connected to each other. Further research could aim at establishing in what way the rationality of our behavior, our negative mental image of darkness, and the resistance to curtailment measures are correlated with each other.

DarkSky has aimed at preserving our connection to darkness, by providing DarkSky sites. However, it can be argued that DarkSky parks do not necessarily increase our accessibility to darkness but actually limit it. While indeed DarkSky parks allow us to become engaged with darkness, they focus on our engagement with starry night skies rather than our engagement with average darkness. In this sense, they reinforce the current situation that we only appreciate exceptional darkness. Furthermore, as Stone (2021a) suggests, we are placing that what we want to preserve outside urban settings. In this sense, Stone argues that DarkSky parks actually decrease our accessibility to darkness, as it suggests that DarkSky sites and urban dense areas cannot co-exist. If one were to agree that DarkSky sites actually make darkness less accessible, it does in this sense also relate back that our cities are designed solely for humans and cause disconnection from the more-than-human world. Placing darkness outside of urban areas would mean that the city is anthropogenic, while everything outside of the city belongs to the more-than-human world.

If we have grown disconnected from the more-than-human world and from darkness, it could also explain why we currently focus solely on limiting the effects of light pollution. As Rathsach and Hvass (2022) have established, humans are the only species that want ALAN. As ALAN is inherently anthropogenic, we also seek to find an anthropogenic solution for the problems that it causes. Because we tend to overlook the complexities of darkness, we try to treat the problems caused by ALAN with solutions on ALAN. However, as the sub-theme suggests, any exploration of darkness' value necessarily involves its relationship with artificial light. It can be argued that the opposite is also true, which we currently fail to address.
4.2 Our current relationship with darkness

div.head: Extending the day into the night
div.p: The banishing of darkness from our cities also becomes evident in how we treat our environments similarly during the day and during the night, despite the differences in social functions that they might have. As an example, I want to highlight a study by Boyce et al. (2000) on perceived safety at a parking lot during the day and night. Their conclusion is that 30 lux provides sufficient lighting to ensure that safety perceptions during the night are as close to the perceptions during the day as possible. Our aim in including this example is not to criticize Boyce et al.'s work on this, but to raise the question as to whether it should be necessary to perceive parking lots as safe during the night as during the day. Li et al. (2015) have conducted research on physiological and psychological responses towards both darkness and nighttime and found that nighttime increased anxiety for fearful stimuli, regardless of illumination level. This implies that, regardless of illumination level, it is logical that we perceive spaces during the night as less safe than during the day; we are after all diurnal species. Additional support for this claim can be found in research by Kalsbeek and Fliers (2013), who show that the body has several hormonal processes that are governed by our internal clock. Using this governing of hormonal processes, an organism is able to ensure adaptation to its time-structured environment. Kalsbeek and Fliers describe that we are different persons at different times of day, as our hormonal balance in our body is inherently different and adjusted to fit time-dependent events. Interestingly, only few authors mention the differences between night and darkness. The theme of darkness being contextual touches upon this by stating that perceptions of darkness are influenced by time. However, it can be argued that it is not darkness which has temporal characteristics, but night. Indeed, darkness can be influenced by seasonal variations (Tainio, 2024) or by the cycle of the moon (Rathsach & Hvass, 2022), however, on a daily basis the temporal variations of darkness are influenced by the setting and rising of the sun. This puts the findings from the thematic analysis in a different light, as several concepts might relate more to night than that of darkness. Further research would be necessary to establish which of the concepts are related to darkness, night, or both.

Despite the contextual differences, we currently aim at extending the day into the night. A possible explanation for this that I suggest can be found in (perceived) affordance theory (Gibson, 1977;Norman, 1988). As darkness decreases our visibility, we are no longer aware of the affordances that an environment offers, as we cannot see them anymore. Lighting our environment the same at night as during the day could thus imply that lighting is used as a design tool to preserve the affordances that we have designed in our environment.

Yet, it raises the question whether it is rational to light our nights. Otto et al. (2014) explained rational behavior as a means of satisfying personal ends. Taking the definition of Otto et al., lighting our environment at night would seem rational. However, as Vuorenmaa et al. (2024) have shown, learning about darkness can shift our thinking. By introducing the general public to the complexities of darkness, but also to the benefits of darkness, it might be possible to shift the rationale for lighting our night. This would shift lighting design to a demand-oriented policy, such as Beaudet et al. (2022) proposed. In such a demand-oriented view, the rational behavior for lighting our nighttime environment would be to only use light when it creates benefits that darkness cannot offer.

div.head: How can we place darkness as a design asset
div.p: As the sub-themes from focusing solely on light pollution will limit the adverse effects of ALAN but does not reflect the benefits that darkness has show, darkness has several benefits. As Dill (2022) explained, the benefits on well-being are a consequence of experiencing natural beauty. A theory that could possibly explain this is Attention-Restoration theory (ART; Kaplan, 1995). ART states that natural scenes can restore the depleted attention span of a person. According to Kaplan, the attention span can be restored using involuntary attention, in other words, fascination. ART could explain why we appreciate exceptional darkness more than average darkness. Exceptional darkness, or in other words, starry night skies, provides high levels of (soft) fascination. They also partially fit Kaplan's definition of extent, another core component of restorative environments, as they show how the environment is constituted to a larger whole, even though they do not offer the possibility of exploring it. The restorative potential of starry night skies can however not be seen apart from darkness, as stars are only visible in darkness. Importantly, as Tainio (2023) has proposed, learning to appreciate average darkness should be a necessity. The question then arises; can mundane darkness provide for the components of ART and then be implemented as a design asset? Further exploration of average darkness through the lens of ART is needed to determine whether it can provide the same benefits as exceptional darkness.

The benefits that darkness provides for increased connectedness can also be seen through a theoretical lens. As Dill (2022) and Challéat et al. (2021) note, dimmed environments allow for deeper connection due to the original forms of conviviality and intimacy that they create. The theoretical lens that could be applied to this is that of Altman's Privacy-Regulation theory (Altman, 1975). As darkness decreases our ability to see others, we might compensate for this through other interpersonal control mechanisms. In this situation, darkness would offer more privacy than we want, but darkness could also offer us the privacy that we seek, which would not result in increased connectedness, but still add to well-being. In any case, Privacy-Regulation theory also offers an interesting lens through which darkness could be explored in further research.

These two theories provide lenses through which darkness as a design asset, as something to design for, can be explored. Stone (2024) proposes that the benefits that darkness offers should be considered as prima facie obligations: moral duties which are binding but can be overridden by stronger moral duties. They argue that positioning darkness in this way makes it a theoretical foundation, instead of an add-on with benefits. In this sense, Stone aims at positioning urban darkness as a form of urban restoration (Stone, 2023). They define urban restoration as the act of restoring not just the consequences of excessive lighting but also repairing the relationship that we have with darkness. Stone thus suggests that our relationship with darkness is broken and needs fixing. Placing urban darkness as a form of urban restoration can, according to Stone, thus increase our understanding of darkness and increase our connectedness with the more-than-human world.

Placing darkness as a design asset creates a human perspective in lighting design. Darkness has certain benefits that light does not possess and including it early onwards in the design can change the objective of designing an environment to include the human benefits needed for the specific situation, be it from either light or darkness. However, placing urban darkness as a form of urban restoration puts a more-than-human perspective in lighting design. Given the multi-faceted value of darkness, perhaps this more-than-human perspective is needed to create a healthy urban environment.

div.head: Curtailment of light or reconciliation with darkness?
div.p: This does not mean that we should seize all ALAN from existence, however. Boyce (2019) has mentioned the benefits of ALAN to be providing visibility, security, safety, promoting nighttime economy, and increasing beauty of places. Indeed, for several of these, darkness cannot provide the benefits that light can. In the case study by Rathsach and Hvass (2022) for example, the city of Anholt used the moon as a light source to provide visibility. However, due to the phasing of the moon, and thus the temporal variations of darkness, on dark nights the moon could not provide for sufficient visibility. This shows that light is certainly needed in some cases. Further evidence that backs this up can be found in studies on traffic accidents, which also specify the need for light at night (Yannis et al., 2013).

Yet, more light is not always positive. Hvass (2024) shows an empirical example where they found that reducing light -creating a more balanced hierarchy of lighting layers -actually increased perceived safety at a Danish tram station. From this example, it can be argued that both light and darkness have benefits for increasing perceived safety, however, these benefits depend on the context of the environment. Furthermore, the section above shows several cases of how darkness has benefits that light cannot create. These examples highlight the contextuality of both light and darkness. Looking at the opinion of the authors from the 24 manuscripts, no one is in favor of completely extinguishing light from our nighttime environment, but all specify that we need to balance light and darkness. In their view the benefits of light cannot be neglected, but darkness also offers potential benefits that we currently ignore.

Both the demand-oriented policy of light (Beaudet et al., 2022) and placing darkness as a form of urban restoration (Stone, 2023) acknowledge that the benefits of light cannot be neglected. Both these strategies aim at giving darkness a moral value. What becomes evident from this research however, is that for any implementation of giving darkness moral value, light should also be considered. Ultimately, the optimal balance between light and darkness is perhaps about visibility, yet the question is what we want to make visible. The more we light the street's surface, the darker the shadows we cast elsewhere.
