Defining this optimal balance between light and dark is the next step in research on our relationship with urban darkness. Hence, the solution will not be to choose between curtailment of light or reconciliation with darkness, but both.

div.head: Steppingstone for future research
div.p: The recency from the 24 manuscripts of the scoping review shows the increased interest in darkness as a research topic, however, it also shows that we are very much in the early stages of darkness research. Research question 2 focused on the types of measurements tools included. It became apparent that most researchers used qualitative tools. Hvass (2024) mentions the importance of including both quantitative and qualitative methods for researching human experience for outdoor lighting. However, if one were to develop a meaningful quantitative tool, in this early stage of research a thorough understanding of the concept is of key importance. Therefore, more qualitative research is needed on topics such as, how the values of light and dark interact with each other, why entering dark places is considered irrational behavior and how this can be overcome, and on other potential benefits of darkness. Eventually, quantitative research is also needed to determine correlational relationships between concepts or values, if one were to develop a measurement tool such as the Art of Darkness (European Commission, 2024) project desires. This scoping review can be considered as a steppingstone for what research is needed in order to provide a thorough understanding of urban darkness.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: The findings of this scoping review should be seen in light of several limitations. As this project focused solely on urban darkness, research on rural or natural darkness was excluded from the search. This made it that the results of the thematic analysis are not impacted by findings on rural darkness. To sketch a more complete story on our relationship with darkness, perhaps a similar scoping review on rural darkness can be interesting, as it allows to check whether the hypothesis that the two types of darkness are too distinct is valid.

Additionally, due to time constraints, the quality of the data entries was not critically reviewed. Another limitation for this scoping review was the search query. The search query was chosen to try and include as many relevant articles as possible, while limiting the amount of irrelevant hits. Using a post-hoc relevance-based search query in Scopus, the first 50 articles were screened when the terms "values", "assumptions", "associations", "perceptions", and "dim*" were separately included. This search revealed no additional manuscripts, however, it can be assumed that there might still be relevant articles outside of the first 50 indicated relevant articles by Scopus.

Another limitation was that the first half of the Title-Abstract screening phase was only done by a single researcher. Because of time constraints, the second researcher did not have time to Title-Abstract screen the entire bulk of articles. Therefore, the decision was made that the first researcher got rid of articles that were completely off topic. This means that there might be some possible interesting entries being incorrectly classified as wrong topic, whether by mistake or resulting from some bias of the first researcher. Additionally, for the second researcher to see which articles were labelled as "wrong topic", blind mode had to be turned off in Rayyan. This made it that the remainder is also limited by bias, as researchers could see each other's decisions.

As this research is a master thesis project, the research is subject to time constraints. This means that the themes developed from the thematic analysis might not represent all data that was present in the manuscripts. With more time on thematic analysis, there might still be other themes developed from the data. Furthermore, it could also be that the current themes as listed are subject to change.

Lastly, the exclusion criteria focused on urban darkness and excluded those articles that were only about the positive aspects of light. As mentioned, both darkness and light provide benefits at night, however, the benefits of light are not taken into consideration for the exclusion criteria of the scoping review. Consequently, this research in itself therefore provides a one-sided view, as the thematic analysis only included authors who are in favor of implementing more darkness in the cities. To provide a more elaborate conceptual model of the values of darkness, also the values of light have to be considered, as darkness and light are complementary to an extent.

div.head: Conclusory remarks
div.p: All in all, this scoping review reveals several insights that can benefit research into the domain of darkness. The thematic analysis revealed the way we currently understand and explain darkness and shows the limitations that are inherent to our current definition of it. Our appreciation of darkness is only for the nocturnal sublime, but not for mundane darkness. With this appreciation, we have placed darkness outside of our cities, as placing it within the city will not grant us the values that we currently aim to seek. In our current understanding of light and dark, we aim at extending the day into the night, but the question is whether this is rational. This behavior has caused us to grow disconnected from darkness and because of this, negative beliefs and associations of darkness stay sustained in society.

Our current focus on lighting intensity and comfort seems to fit and feed the ignorance towards darkness. Perhaps it is time to move away from evaluating lighting itself and instead focus on the aesthetics and functions of the environment, and how light and darkness can contribute to this.

This scoping review does however not imply that we should seize all artificial light from existence. As humans, we actually do benefit from light at night, albeit in the right context. Several benefits of light cannot be met with total darkness, making light a necessity in some situations. However, we should focus on creating a more natural balance. One that allows us to regain connection with the natural rhythms present in our cities. Through implementation of darkness in our design principles, we can aim at developing places which include benefits from both light and dark, and are more aligned with these natural rhythms of the night.

In order to do so, we should focus on developing a holistic understanding of light and darkness combined. Research on light is in a further stadium than that of darkness at this point in time, therefore it is important to create a quantitative research tool which reflects the values of darkness. With quantitative research tools for both light and darkness, we can validate the complementary and contradictory relationships between light and dark. All in all, this research aims to highlight a sense of urgency in re-establishing our connection with darkness.
